title: Your Lease Expires in 60 Days. The Landlord Knows It.
excerpt: Working with clients right now who are getting squeezed because they waited too long to look at their options. Here is what is actually happening — and what you can still do about it.
metaTitle: 60 Days to Lease Expiry: How Landlords Exploit Panic and What to Do | Your Office Space
metaDescription: Business owners are signing bad lease renewals right now because they ran out of time. Here is what is really happening in Newcastle, and what you can still do about it.
author: Joe Kelley
body:
The call came in last week. A business owner in Newcastle, lease expires in seven weeks. The landlord's agent had called with new terms: rent increase of 18%, no negotiation room, 30 days to sign or vacate.

He felt trapped. He had not looked at the market. He did not have time to move. The agent knew it.

That is not a coincidence. That is how it is designed to work.

## The leverage is gone before you realise it

Most business owners do not wake up to the fact that they have no negotiating position until the lease expiry is close enough to feel real. By then, the landlord already knows it too.

Here is what I am seeing right now in Newcastle:

Landlords are pricing renewals at whatever the market will bear — which, in a tight market, is often well above what comparable spaces are actually renting for. Why? Because they know most tenants will not have time to move, will not have a credible alternative, and will sign rather than face the chaos of relocating a business in 60 days.

The agent on the other end of that call has one job: get the tenant to commit before they have a chance to think. Early renewal incentives, below-market rates for a short period, a handwritten note from the landlord — whatever it takes to get the signature before the window closes.

And most tenants, under pressure, sign.

## The landlord is not the enemy — but he is not your friend either

I want to be clear about something. Working with landlords is part of what we do. A good landlord relationship is worth protecting. But a landlord who knows you have no alternative is not negotiating with you. He is dictating to you.

The business owner I mentioned above? We ran a quick market check on three comparable spaces in the same precinct. Two were available, one at a lower rent than he is currently paying, another with genuine incentives. We contacted both agents, got proper briefings, and put one landlord on notice that there was a credible alternative.

The 18% rent increase became 4%.

That did not happen because the landlord suddenly became generous. It happened because we created a situation where the landlord had something to lose.

## Why 60 days is the worst possible time to be doing this

Here is what happens when your lease expiry is genuinely close:

**You cannot run a proper process.** A credible relocation or alternative premises search takes weeks — to identify spaces, arrange inspections, get comparable data, and negotiate. Sixty days, with a business to run, is not enough time to do any of it properly.

**You have no leverage.** The landlord can see exactly how much time you have. Every conversation, every letter, every piece of communication from his agent will reflect that knowledge. You are negotiating with your hands tied.

**You will pay a premium on everything.** Removalists, fitout costs, downtime, lease establishment costs — all of it spikes when you are moving under pressure. The rent savings you might have negotiated in a proper process get eaten up by the cost of rushing.

**Your business suffers.** Your team notices uncertainty. Clients notice uncertainty. You are making property decisions under pressure that should be made from a position of clarity.

## What you can still do at 60 days

If you are reading this and your lease is close — do not panic, but move fast.

**Right now:** Find out exactly when your lease expires. Read the expiry clause and any option provisions. Find out if you have already missed an option exercise window.

**This week:** Get a market view on your current rent. What are comparable spaces renting for in your precinct and surrounds? If you are paying above market, you have grounds to push back regardless of where you are in the process.

**If you have any remaining time:** Run a brief on one or two alternative premises. You do not have to move. You do not have to be serious. But knowing what else is available changes the conversation.

**Get a lease review.** If you have not had your current lease reviewed by someone who is working for you — not the landlord's solicitor, not the agent — do it now. Make-good clauses, rent review mechanisms, option terms: these are the things that determine how much you are actually exposed to.

## The 6-12 month rule is not a platitude

I know I talk about this a lot. But I keep seeing the same pattern: business owners who started early end up with better spaces, better terms, and real negotiating power. The ones who waited are paying for it.

If your lease expires in the next 12 months and you have not started looking at your options, start today. Not because moving is inevitable — it is often not the right call. But because the only way to genuinely negotiate from a position of strength is to have one.

If you are already in that 60-day window, call us. We are working with businesses in exactly this situation right now, and there is almost always more you can do than you think.

The landlord's agent already knows your expiry date. You should know your options.
